Voters Guide

2026 Candidate Scorecard

The 2026 Equality Ohio Candidate Scorecard examines multiple critical races — including the statewide elections for Governor, U.S. Senate, Attorney General, Secretary of State, and the Ohio Supreme Court, plus key congressional and Statehouse contests — helping Ohioans make informed choices at the ballot box this November.

“Ohio’s LGBTQ+ communities are counting on voters to show up for them this election. This scorecard is a tool to help people see who is committed to equality and who is standing in the way of it. Every vote is a statement about the kind of Ohio we want to build.”

— Dwayne Steward, CEO and Executive Director of Equality Ohio and the Equality Ohio Education Fund

Design preview — candidate portraits and the letter-grade badge graphics from the live scorecard are pending assets, so grades are not shown on the write-ups below. See every grade in the downloadable scorecard PDF.

General Election Scoring

What do candidate grades mean?

All candidates were assessed based on a variety of factors related to their support for LGBTQ+ equality and inclusion, including their legislative records (if they have previously held office), overall career track records, public statements, campaign platforms and other accomplishments.

Judicial candidates were evaluated with the additional criteria of their rulings, independence from partisan politics and the consistency of their judicial philosophy.

Candidate scores are intended to provide voters with information, not serve as an endorsement or punishment.

How to interpret letter grades

A+

Champion of equality: Sustained, strong record of support for LGBTQ+ Ohioans

A

Strong record of support for LGBTQ+ Ohioans

B

Mostly strong record or insufficient record but supportive public statements

C

Mixed record or no record and no public statements

D

Mostly poor record or no record and public statements opposing LGBTQ+ equality

F

Sustained, poor record opposing LGBTQ+ equality

Statewide Races

U.S. Senator

SB

Sherrod Brown

U.S. Senate
  • He voted against the Defense of Marriage Act in 1996 and was a staunch advocate for the Equality Act.
  • He has long supported legislation to expand nondiscrimination protections and defend marriage equality and civil rights for all.
  • In his current campaign, he has publicly voiced support for equality for all Ohioans.
JH

Jon Husted

U.S. Senate
  • He has a longstanding record opposing LGBTQ+ equality, including previously voting to ban same-sex marriage.
  • He criticized Governor DeWine’s veto of legislation banning gender-affirming care for transgender minors.
  • He championed HB 8, Ohio’s “Don’t Say Gay/Trans” law.

Ohio Governor

AA

Amy Acton

Governor
  • She has voiced support for reproductive freedom, public education, and workers’ and union rights.
  • Her campaign wrote to the press that she, “will always stand up for Ohioans, including the LGBT community. As governor, she is committed to standing up to discrimination and ensuring all Ohioans receive equal protection under the law.”

Following a remark on June 30, 2026, her grade changed from “A” to “B”, reflecting unresolved concerns about support for trans Ohioans.

VR

Vivek Ramaswamy

Governor
  • He supports bans on gender-affirming care and has referred to transgender identity as a “mental health disorder.”
  • He has characterized the broader LGBTQ+ movement as “cult-like” and aligned himself with national culture war messaging targeting LGBTQ+ inclusion.
  • He has criticized diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives and supports restrictions on reproductive healthcare access.

Ohio Secretary of State

AR

Allison Russo

Secretary of State
  • She is a leading advocate, voting against HB 8, Ohio’s “Don’t Say Gay/Trans” law.
  • She has consistently supported policies promoting LGBTQ+ equality, inclusion, and personal freedom throughout her time in the legislature including co-sponsoring the Ohio Fairness Act and Conversion Therapy Ban.
  • She advocated against Issue 1 in 2023, which would have required a supermajority vote for future citizen-led ballot initiatives.
RS

Robert Sprague

Secretary of State
  • While in the legislature, he voted for the Ohio Pastor Protection Act, allowing clergy and religious organizations to refuse to solemnize same-sex marriages or to use their property for those ceremonies.
  • He has publicly stated that marriage is “between one man and one woman” and disagreed with the Supreme Court when it struck down the Defense of Marriage Act.
  • He has publicly stated that affirming trans youth is child abuse.
  • He has emphasized restricting voter access by expanding photo-ID requirements and eliminating ballot drop boxes.

Ohio Attorney General

JK

John Kulewicz

Attorney General
  • While on Upper Arlington City Council, he voted for nondiscrimination protections for LGBTQ+ residents in housing, public accommodations, and employment.
  • He publicly supports civil rights protections for LGBTQ+ Ohioans.
  • He brings 44 years of legal experience, including arguing cases before the U.S. Supreme Court and courts across Ohio.
KF

Keith Faber

Attorney General
  • He voted for Ohio’s 2004 Defense of Marriage Act, which prohibited the recognition of same-sex marriages and reduced protections for LGBTQ+ Ohioans in nonmarital relationships.
  • He voted for the Ohio Pastor Protection Act, allowing clergy and religious organizations to refuse to solemnize same-sex marriages or to use their property for those ceremonies.

Ohio Supreme Court

JB

Jennifer Brunner

Ohio Supreme Court
  • She dissented when the Court allowed enforcement of Ohio’s ban on gender-affirming care.
  • She has consistently defended individual liberties and equal protection under the law.
CO

Colleen O’Donnell

Ohio Supreme Court
  • She has not established a public history of advocating for LGBTQ+ rights or civil rights protections.
  • Her record reflects a consistently more conservative judicial approach.
MZ

Marilyn Zayas

Ohio Supreme Court
  • Her demonstrated commitment to fairness, equal access to the courts, and impartial application of the law earns her high marks on equality.
  • She authored the unanimous First District Court of Appeals opinion affirming a same-sex couple’s right to receive the same legal benefits associated with marriage.
  • She was appointed three times within a 40-day span by Ohio’s Chief Justice to sit on the Ohio Supreme Court, an uncommon distinction that underscores her expertise and the respect she has earned across the judiciary.
DH

Dan Hawkins

Ohio Supreme Court
  • He joined the Court’s majority allowing enforcement of Ohio’s ban on gender-affirming care for transgender minors to proceed.
  • He joined the Court’s majority in overturning the First District Court of Appeals decision which affirmed a same-sex couple’s right to receive the same legal benefits associated with marriage.
  • His broader record includes limited direct commentary on LGBTQ+ issues.
Champions of Equality

Eight candidates earned the top designation

Candidates are scaled on an A–F letter grade, with eight candidates receiving the top designation of “Champion of Equality”: Jennifer Brunner (Ohio Supreme Court), Allison Russo (Secretary of State), Greg Landsman (CD01), Emilia Sykes (CD13), Christine Cockley (HD06), Mike Baker (HD52), Jeff Givan (HD78), and Arienne Childrey (HD84).

Voter Resources

Additional nonpartisan voter resources

Make Your Plan to Vote

Three dates to write down

  • October 5: Deadline to register or update your registration.
  • October 6: Early in-person and absentee voting begins.
  • November 3: Election Day in Ohio! Polls open 6:30am – 7:30pm.
Registration & Polling Place

Check your registration and know before you vote!
